extracted.intended_audience: employers, workers, labor lawyers, policy makers, and other stakeholders assessing worker classification under the FLSA
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the FLSA economic-reality factors to determine whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor, focusing on permanence, exclusivity, control (including scheduling, supervision, and economic control), and compliance obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusivity of relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognizing that exclusivity weighs in favor of the worker being an employee, but an exclusive relationship alone is not determinative; conversely, working multiple jobs or not relying on a single employer for income does not automatically indicate independent contractor status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look at exclusivity among other relevant factors (including opportunity for profit/loss and permanence). Courts have held that sporadic or irregular work and multiple employers do not necessarily remove a worker from employee status (e.g., Silk; Superior Care). Consider whether multiple jobs are a business choice or a financial necessity—many low-wage workers hold multiple jobs out of necessity, which does not demonstrate business independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of permanence of the work relationship (§795.105(b)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Work relationships that are indefinite in duration or continuous weigh in favor of employee status; routine or automatic contractual renewals can indicate permanence and an indefinite working arrangement associated with employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the relationship is characterized by continuity and regularity rather than sporadic, project-based engagements. Example: A cook who prepares meals continuously and exclusively for an entertainment venue with regularly scheduled events indicates a high degree of permanence and favors employee status; by contrast, a cook who provides intermittent, market-seeking specialty meals and rejects work when busy indicates a sporadic, nonexclusive relationship favoring independent contractor status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and degree of control (§795.110(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Control is a factor in the economic reality test analyzed as part of the totality of the circumstances; the focus should be on the potential employer's nature and degree of control (not elevated to a 'core' factor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the potential employer exerts control that is probative of the worker's economic dependence. The inquiry centers on whether the employer controls meaningful economic aspects of the work relationship. Courts and historical Department practice concentrate on employer control (e.g., right to control manner and means). Do not assign fixed weights—more indicia of employer control favors employee status; more indicia of worker control favors independent contractor status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling (employer control over worker's schedule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the employer sets the worker's schedule is a fact relevant to the control factor, but a worker's ability to set their own schedule by itself provides only minimal evidence of independent contractor status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate scheduling freedom against other employer controls. Scheduling flexibility is common to both employees and independent contractors and is not significant alone—courts have found employees despite schedule flexibility. Consider whether the employer limits hours available, sequences or paces work, or disciplines workers for declining work; such measures can indicate employer control even where schedule flexibility exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision over performance and assignment of work
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the potential employer supervises the worker's performance, assigns work, or otherwise directs the manner of work is probative of control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include supervision mediated by technology and other modern forms of oversight when assessing control. Direct workplace supervision (e.g., setting tasks, directing methods) is an obvious form of control, but absence of overt supervision does not preclude other indicia (reserved rights, economic controls) from indicating employee status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worker's ability to work for others
rubrics_metrics.description: A worker's ability to work for other employers or clients is a relevant consideration; however, working for multiple employers is not dispositive and does not automatically signal independent contractor status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the ability to work for others reflects genuine business independence or is simply a financial necessity. Courts have held that employees may work for more than one employer without losing employee status; this factor should be weighed alongside control over economic aspects and other indicia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved control / reserved rights to control
rubrics_metrics.description: Employer reserved rights to control (even if not actively exercised) can be probative of employer control and of employee status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore reserved contractual rights or retained authority; the absence of obvious workplace control does not mean the employer lacks reserved powers that demonstrate control over economic aspects of the relationship. The Department retains reserved control in regulation text because such reserved rights may, in some situations, be probative of the economic reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control over economic aspects of the work relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Employer control over economic elements—such as pricing of services, provision of leads, defining territory, and determining clientele—is particularly probative of whether workers are economically dependent and thus employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the employer sets prices, supplies customers/leads, restricts territory, or otherwise controls core business operations that affect a worker's ability to operate as an independent business. Case examples include insurance firms controlling pricing and leads and clubs controlling prices and clientele for dancers; such economic controls supported employee findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with legal, safety, contractual, or quality control obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether actions taken by a potential employer related to legal, safety, contractual, or quality control obligations indicate control depends on context: actions taken solely to comply with specific applicable law/regulation are not indicative of control, but actions that go beyond mere legal compliance and instead implement the employer's own compliance methods, safety, quality control, contractual, or customer service standards may be indicative of control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between (a) measures taken solely to meet a specific, applicable federal/state/tribal/local law or regulation (not indicative of control) and (b) employer-imposed methods or standards beyond such legal requirements (may be probative of employer control if they indicate the worker is not performing entrepreneurial risk/assumption). Examples: A required background check per Medicaid is not indicative of control; extensive provider qualifications or employer-mandated training beyond licensure requirements may be probative. Requiring proof of legally-mandated insurance is not indicative, but mandating the insurer to be used may be probative.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement for a 'substantial control' threshold; totality of the circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulation does not require 'substantial' control as a legal prerequisite; rather, the totality of the circumstances must be weighed—substantial control can indicate employee status but is not a predetermined requisite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have said it's impossible to assign specific, invariably applied weight to each factor. Consider all indicia: more indicia of employer control favors employee status; more indicia of worker control favors independent contractor status. Avoid rigid bright-line tests; evaluate how multiple forms of control and economic dependence interact in each case.
